images.caption: Figure 1:Types of In-domain and OOD Tasks:While VLAs often perform well for in-domain tasks seen during training, their success rates tend to deteriorate when encountering unseen language instructions (left,38.2%→14.2%\text{38.2\%}\rightarrow\text{14.2\%})[10]or unseen task environments (right,70.2%→36.0%\text{70.2\%}\rightarrow\text{36.0\%})[9]. Recent methods focus on inference-time steering for VLAs to achieve better generalization to these OOD tasks without extensive data collection and expensive retraining.

Figure 2:Real-Robot Experiment forTape in ToolboxTask (OOD Environment):This task is challenging for the base VLA (π0\pi_{0}[2]) because the tape was never seen during training.(Left)Rephrasecorrectly grasps the tape but often collides with the side of the toolbox.(Middle)Non-adaptiveR​L2RL^{2}inaccurately approaches the tape, as it unnecessarily steers already-accurate VLA action samples.(Right)AdaptiveR​L2RL^{2}relies on accurate VLA samples to approach the tape, then steers actions to lift the tape high enough to avoid collision, when failure is preemptively detected via Conformal Prediction (CP)[11].

Figure 3:Test-time Scaling Laws (Steering Improves Failure States but Degrades Success States):We observe that the action error between ground truth and predicted VLA actions (π0\pi_{0}[2]) consistently decreases as we scale the number of action samples across different offline RL and baseline steering approaches.
Most notably, compositional steering (R​L2RL^{2}) andRBF[14]exhibit the best scaling property due to their ability to generate diverse yet high-quality action samples during failure. However, they perform poorly compared to baseline approaches during success states, prompting the need to apply steering adaptively.

Figure 4:R​L2RL^{2}Framework (Flow-Matching VLAs):(i)For flow-matching-based VLAs likeπ0\pi_{0}[2], given language instructions and observations,R​L2RL^{2}first extracts action expert latents (ete_{t}) from its frozen VLA action expert.(ii)The latentsete_{t}is fed into the RL flow-matching steering policy, which provides guidance velocitiesVR​LV_{RL}that are composed with the VLA flow velocitiesVV​L​AV_{VLA}at each flow-matching step to generate diverse and high-quality action candidates.(iii)In parallel,ete_{t}is passed into a failure detection module that determines whether steering should be enabled: if failure is detected,R​L2RL^{2}composes the VLA and RL velocities; otherwise, it falls back to the base VLA action distribution.(iv)Finally, a verifier scores the generated candidates and selects the best action to execute
(*for autoregressive VLAs like OpenVLA[17], we use Gaussian perturbation[19]to perform RL compositional steering).

Figure 12:Results of our Real-Robot Experiments:We curate two in-domain and two challenging OOD task environments to compareR​L2RL^{2}against baseline approaches on-hardware.
AdaptiveR​L2RL^{2}achieves an average of +17.5% overRephrase[20]baseline, highlighting its robustness to failure modes present in the base VLA.
Similarly, adaptiveR​L2RL^{2}achieves an average of +14.2% over non-adaptiveR​L2RL^{2}, highlighting the importance of steering only during failures.

Figure 13:Real-Robot Experiment forScrewdriver in ToolboxTask (OOD Environment):This task is challenging for the base VLA (π0\pi_{0}[2]) because the screwdriver was never seen during training and the scene includes a tape distractor.(Left)Rephrasecorrectly grasps the screwdriver but mistakenly carries the screwdriver to the tape instead of into the box.(Middle)Non-adaptiveR​L2RL^{2}inaccurately approaches the screwdriver, as it unnecessarily steers already-accurate VLA action samples.(Right)AdaptiveR​L2RL^{2}relies on accurate VLA samples to approach the screwdriver, then performs compositional steering to guide the samples away from the distractor object and towards the toolbox, when failure is preemptively detected via Conformal Prediction (CP)[11].

Figure 17:Comparison of SAFE Failure Probabilities and CoVer Scores:For bothπ0\pi_{0}andπ0.5\pi_{0.5}as the base VLA, we visualize SAFE[11]failure probabilities (left) and CoVer[20]VLM normalized score (right) against normalized episode progress.
The solid lines and their corresponding colored bands represent the mean and standard deviation across a large number of episodesnn.
SAFE acts as an effective intervention trigger because success and failure scores are easily separable, whereas CoVer is less effective as an intervention trigger because success and failure scores are very correlated.
